job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Femi. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take the 7:10 train to Carrow Technical University, because I still live with my mother in her two-room flat across town. I'm on a master's in manufacturing engineering. After lectures I spend a couple of hours in the workshop on the lathe, then I do one application on the train home. Mum cleans offices at night, so we pass each other at the door most days.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mechanical engineering, a pass, an average one. My final project was redesigning a gearbox test rig, and my supervisor said the mechanics were sound but the report was thin. I didn't do an internship, because the ones I knew of were unpaid and I had to help mum with the bills. I owe about twenty-seven thousand and I don't expect anyone to pay it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. Most things that get called a revolution turn out to be a new button on the same machine. I'd tell my cousin that the factories I know still run on bolts, grease and people who turn up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm in the same spot as today. Few openings for mechanical graduates near here, a pass degree and no internship. I'd be quietly worried about money and about mum's knees, because she can't clean offices forever. It's not about AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep helping at my uncle's garage on Saturdays, and apply for the graduate programme at the pump plant on the industrial estate every autumn. I'd also visit the plant's open day and talk to a supervisor face to face, which works better for me than an online form. I wouldn't change anything about how I do my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, not scared. It's a slow kind of worry, like a dripping tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said face to face works better. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not good at selling myself on a form. When I'm standing next to a machine and someone asks me how it works, I can answer. An online form asks about my 'passion', and I don't know what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she'll get ill and I won't be able to cover the rent. She's 52 and she carries the vacuum all night. If I land a job at the plant, that's the first thing I'd fix.

say: I'd say most revolutions are a **new button** on the same machine.
I'd tell my cousin factories still run on bolts, grease and punctual people.
think: Nothing changes for me: few mechanical openings near here, a **pass degree** and no internship.
I worry about money and about my mum's **knees**.
do: Finish the master's and help at my uncle's **garage** on Saturdays.
Apply to the **pump plant** graduate programme each autumn and visit its open day.
Keep working the way I do now, with no AI tools.
feel: **Tired**, not scared; the worry is slow, like a dripping tap.

Mentions the pump plant by name: one realistic target in a thin local market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be careful, because jobs that sit at a desk will change first. I'd say it to my classmates and at home: write down what your day actually is, and see what a machine could do. I'm not against change, I just want to see that it works before I rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think design offices will need fewer juniors, and those are the jobs graduates like me apply for. Factories and workshops move more slowly, so there's a bit of room. But the factory's planning and ordering get done by software, and that lowers the number of graduate posts. I'm in the awkward middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for roles on the shop floor side of manufacturing: maintenance, quality testing, production support. I'd take whatever the pump plant offers, even a technician post, and work upwards. I'd try to learn the new software only if the plant gives me training, because I don't want to guess at tools on my own. I'd also keep the Saturday shifts at the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit gloomy. I'm not a person who jumps early, so I'd feel behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel behind. Who's ahead of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My classmate Aiyana is already using three different AI tools for her reports, and she gets better marks for the same work. I look at her screen and think it should be me. But I don't like changing how I work until I've seen it prove itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a technician job if it paid less than a graduate post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, immediately. A paid job on a shop floor is worth more than an unpaid wait for a design job that may never come. My mum would breathe out for the first time in a year.

Factories move slower, but planning and ordering are done by software, so I'm in an awkward middle.

fieldNote: His **resistance** shows: he waits for proof and for employer-provided training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd say nobody is ready, not companies, not the council, not families like mine. I'd say we need a plan from the government, because people like my mum can't plan around this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. The master's finishes in a year, and I'd be walking into a market where thinking work is done by software. Even if robots take until 2031 for hands-on work, the planning and paperwork around factories would go sooner, and my pass degree wouldn't help. I'd have debt and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get onto a shop floor before it happens: any production or maintenance job, even temporary, and stay close to machines. I'd stop thinking about design roles. I'd keep helping at my uncle's garage and ask him about a place there. And I'd cut spending to the bone: no train pass except for lectures, no phone upgrade, mum and I would cook together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like a weight on my shoulders. I can sit still but my stomach is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said mum and you would cook together. What would your evenings be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet. She'd come home at six in the morning from the office cleaning, and I'd have breakfast ready. We'd watch the news, and she'd say something calm like 'we've had worse'. I'm not sure we have, but it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd phone the loan company and ask what the options are. I know that sounds basic, but I've never done it, and I'd want to know before the payments start.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready**: not companies, not the council, not families like mine.
I'd say we need a clear government plan.
think: The master's finishes in a year, and I'd walk into a market where **thinking work** is done by software.
I'd have debt and no savings, and a pass degree wouldn't help.

S2.quote: Nobody is ready, not companies, not the council, not families like mine.
fieldNote: Falls back on **hands-on** work and family ties, matching the card's 2031 robot gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is something I could plan around, but I'd still say it's too fast. I'd say it to my uncle and my mum: we've got a few years, so use them. I wouldn't argue online, I'm not that kind of person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get maybe three years of work before the thinking work is automated and about five before robots reach the shop floor. That's enough to pay off a good chunk of debt if I'm paid decently. If I'm not, then I'm in the same position as in the two-year one, only slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and put everything into getting a stable factory job near home. I'd save 100 a month, pay off the smaller loan first and learn how to fix the machines, not only design them. I'd take any course the plant offered on automation because I'd rather be the one who looks after a robot than the one it replaces. I'd keep helping at the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the two-year version, but there's a slow dread under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather look after the robot. What would that job be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maintenance on automated lines. The pump plant has two robot arms already, and when one breaks, the supplier sends a man from three hours away. I'd want to be that man, but local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody hires me at the plant. They've never advertised a graduate post, only apprentices. If they don't take me, I'd have to move, and I don't want to leave my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd say it will probably be fine for most people. I'd say plan for it, don't panic, and don't believe everyone who says they know exactly how it goes. I'd tell my cousin to put some money away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but hopeful. I'd have time to get a job, clear most of the debt, and learn a trade skill like machine maintenance or electrical work. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a steady job and a decade of experience. The worry is the first job, still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a factory job, save 150 a month, and over ten years study for a maintenance or controls qualification. I'd also like to buy a small flat with my mum. I'd keep working with the tools I know and let others find the problems before I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, though not completely. I'd feel I have enough time to make a plan, and that's a rare feeling for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let others find the problems first. Is that a good strategy here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's served me well. I don't like being first, because first people make mistakes at their own cost. With ten years I can afford to wait and watch, as long as I don't wait too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be a signal that you'd waited too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plant started asking for skills I don't have, or if my classmates were all in jobs and I wasn't. I'd see it in the job posts before anywhere else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have debt, a pass degree and no time to find my feet. What would help is a firm that takes graduates and trains them on the job, and some kind of help for the loan if the jobs vanish. And more places for people like me to meet employers in person, not through forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of hard work or of change. I just need to see it's real first. Plenty of people like me get overlooked because we don't talk much, and we're good in a workshop.
